P12.6 (T4): Geometric ﬁnite-map functoriality and conductor descent
Establish compatibility of independently geometric singular psh cones, envelopes and Monge–
Ampère products with ﬁnite maps, normalization and conductor descent. Finite restric-
tion, ideal-cone extrema, normal-domain norm traces, ﬁnite-ﬂat determinant traces and their
tower/gauge rules are known. They do not identify the geometric operators; an unrestricted
continuous degree trace is obstructed.

ENTIRE ORIGINAL FAMILY DOSSIER
6     A geometric local theory on singular germs
Active items: P12.2, P12.3, P12.4, P12.5, P12.6. Status: Open in the residual scope.

6.1   Atomic targets
P12.2 (T4): An independently geometric singular valuative psh cone
On the intrinsic normalized boundary of an excellent singular or nonnormal germ, construct
a valuative psh class with independent geometric meaning and the correct smooth-germ spe-
cialization. Identify its relation to the existing ideal-generated cone. Deﬁning another order-
theoretic completion does not by itself supply that identiﬁcation.

P12.3 (T4): An independently geometric singular envelope theory
Construct obstacle envelopes for the independently geometric singular psh cone, establish
their positivity and the appropriate regularity, and compare them with the complete ideal-
psh envelope already known on reduced-curve links.

P12.4 (T5): Model-independent bounded singular-local products
Construct bounded mixed Monge–Ampère products on singular and nonnormal normalized
local boundaries, with model independence, the correct intersection comparison, locality and
continuity. The existing compact boundary construction alone supplies no such product.

P12.5 (T5): Finite energy on singular local boundaries
Construct an energy functional, ﬁnite-energy class, and its Monge–Ampère calculus for excel-
lent singular and nonnormal germs. Specify reference data, changes of primary gauge, and
the relation between bounded approximation and ﬁnite-energy limits.

P12.6 (T4): Geometric ﬁnite-map functoriality and conductor descent
Establish compatibility of independently geometric singular psh cones, envelopes and Monge–
Ampère products with ﬁnite maps, normalization and conductor descent. Finite restric-
tion, ideal-cone extrema, normal-domain norm traces, ﬁnite-ﬂat determinant traces and their
tower/gauge rules are known. They do not identify the geometric operators; an unrestricted
continuous degree trace is obstructed.

6.2   What constitutes a solution
The requested geometric cone, envelopes, bounded products, ﬁnite energy and map compat-
ibility are separate targets. Prove their smooth-germ specialization, primary-gauge changes
and normalization/conductor rules. Do not identify an ideal-generated order completion with
a geometric pluripotential theory without an additional comparison theorem.

6.3   Full statement and detailed state of the art
Finite-map progress is now available in Book Section 70.2: continuous positive trace over
normal targets without ﬂatness, ﬁber extrema for arbitrary ﬁnite maps onto their exact im-
ages, and the exact conductor criterion for continuous descent. The ideal-generated cones
are explicit; their identiﬁcation with a geometric singular psh class and compatibility with
envelopes and Monge–Ampère products are not claimed. This settles the valuative transfer
layer of P12.6 and narrows its remaining geometric target.

Problem 6.1. Extend the normalized local theory of Book Chapter 70 from smooth complex
germs to excellent singular and nonnormal germs. On the normalized boundary of Book
Section 70.1.1, construct, when possible, psh functions, envelopes, bounded products, ﬁnite
energy, and ﬁnite-map functoriality.
    The normalizing-boundary part is resolved in arbitrary dimension. Book Theorem 70.1.2
gives the intrinsic centered ray space and its nonempty compact sections for all m-primary
ideals, with exact change (Book 70.7a). Book Theorem 70.1.3 presents each section as a
quotient of the separated normalization branches. Fibers are singletons where the conductor
has ﬁnite value; on its inﬁnite-value stratum, equality of restrictions to the conductor quo-
tient is the precise identiﬁcation rule. Nonprimary ideals deﬁne the partial sections (Book
70.7e), which can be noncompact. Nilpotents are invisible to these semivaluations, and a zero-
dimensional local reduction has empty centered cone. This settles P12.1, while P12.2–P12.6
retain their separate psh, envelope, product, energy and ﬁnite-map targets. It does not assert
an intersection theory or resolution in positive characteristic.
    In dimension one, this construction reduces to a ﬁnite branch set. By Book Theorem 70.1.4,
the link normalized by an m-primary ideal a is the ﬁnite discrete set of normalization branches
q above the closed point, with point

Changing the primary ideal rescales this same branch set by the exact cocycle (Book Chap-
ter 70, †). In particular, branches cannot be indexed only by irreducible components: the irre-
ducible node in Book Example 70.1.4 has one minimal prime and two normalization branches.
    There is also an exact link-level ﬁnite-map formula. Book Proposition 70.1.2 applies to
an arbitrary ﬁnite local homomorphism of reduced Nagata curve germs, without injectivity.
When a source branch has ramiﬁcation index e over a target branch, both its order and the
order of the extended ideal aS acquire the factor e, so normalization cancels it. The resulting
restriction maps are compatible with composition and change of primary ideal. They need
not be surjective; this remains a link-level result.
    There is now also an exact conductor-controlled ideal-level range. Book Proposition 70.1.3
shows that every suﬃciently deep integral vector of branch orders is realized by one downstairs
nonzerodivisor generating an m-primary ideal. Consequently Book Theorem 70.1.5 identiﬁes
the principal-ideal proﬁles with the strictly negative rational orthant, their uniform closure
with all nonpositive functions on the ﬁnite link, and their raw obstacle envelope with min{φ, 0}.
The monotone boundary is sharp: all nonpositive proﬁles admit increasing approximation
from below, whereas a proﬁle with a zero branch coordinate cannot be a decreasing limit of
primary-ideal proﬁles. These conclusions concern only the explicitly deﬁned ideal-function
family.
    There is now also a complete order-theoretic calculus for the book-local ideal-closure can-
didate. By Book Theorem 70.1.6, its continuous ideal-psh class is every ﬁnite nonpositive
function on the branch link, and its decreasing completion is every extended nonpositive func-
tion. Equivalently, it is the intrinsic cone of nonpositive degree-one homogeneous functions
on the unnormalized branch-valuation rays. Changing the primary ideal merely changes the
cross-section and obeys an exact cocycle; ﬁnite local maps pull the class back, preserve prin-
cipal models, and commute with the envelope min{φ, 0}. Their pullback image is exactly the
ﬁber-constant subclass; pullback is injective precisely for a surjective branch map and sur-
jective precisely for an injective branch map, while surjective branch maps act isometrically
on the continuous class. On the completed lattices, ﬁberwise supremum and inﬁmum give
explicit left and right adjoints to pullback, with −∞ and zero as the two empty-ﬁber conven-
tions; the resulting source-side composites are the least ﬁber-constant majorant and greatest
ﬁber-constant minorant, so their ﬁxed points are exactly the functions descending through

    The label “ideal-psh” is a scope marker, not a comparison theorem. No argument here iden-
tiﬁes this closure with an independently constructed singular nef-b-divisor, CLD, or complex-
analytic psh cone, and it supplies no Monge–Ampère product or energy class. Thus the curve
case of the explicit ideal-closure and envelope calculus is complete, but it does not by itself
discharge the full psh or envelope atoms.
    The most direct comparison can nevertheless be computed exactly whenever the ﬁnite
normalization is a union of q closed discs, is an isomorphism away from one point, and its
conductor contains suﬃciently high separated branch powers. By Book Theorem 70.1.9, a
homogeneous proﬁle c ∈ [−∞, 0]q has a literal logarithmic radial extension which is classically
psh if and only if it has one which is CLD-v2 psh, and the exact subcone is

The positive direction forms the normalized tuple whose retained components are the mono-
mials tki i , whose −∞-components are zero, and descends it through the conductor to one
analytic function; scaled logarithms and a decreasing limit then give all remaining slopes.
For the converse, a zero branch forces a nonnegative nodal value by upper semicontinuity;
any simultaneously negative branch then contradicts its closed-disc Shilov maximum prin-
ciple. Hence the mixed-zero ideal proﬁle (−1, 0) is excluded, while every proﬁle with all
coordinates strictly negative or −∞ does extend. The conductor realizes the required branch-
wise monomials by single downstairs analytic functions, so this supplies the exact branch-
compatibility rule throughout the stated disc-normalized curve range. The ordinary multinode
theorem Book Theorem 70.1.10 records the explicit coordinate-ring instance. At the oppo-
site extreme, the unibranch cusp in Book Example 70.1.9 has conductor t2 Khti, and its cone
{0} ∪ [−∞, 0) = [−∞, 0] contains every nonpositive radial proﬁle; the mixed-zero obstruction
is therefore genuinely multibranch. The result does not decide whether a diﬀerent boundary-
trace comparison exists, or treat a singular germ outside this normalization-and-conductor
range.
    There is a genuine, but diﬀerent, global boundary case. Over an algebraically closed
ﬁeld of characteristic zero, the global trivially-valued framework used in [BJ23, §2] treats an
integral projective variety without initially assuming normality: it supplies a global psh class,
its ﬁnite-energy space and energy, and a Monge–Ampère operator with dense ﬁnite-energy
image. Exact surjectivity there is equivalent to the envelope property, which that source
records in the smooth case. This global construction neither selects a normalized link for an
excellent local germ nor supplies the curve-local conductor realization above, local bounded
products, or the required local ﬁnite-map formula. It therefore does not discharge any part
of Problem 6.1.
    The remaining programme tests higher-dimensional normal crossings, quotient singulari-
ties, and purely inseparable universal homeomorphisms. Any claim of independence of psh
or intersection constructions from boundary choices must respect the established radial com-
parison and conductor quotient. Relative b-divisors can be deﬁned on suitable model sys-
tems, but beyond the normalized boundary and, in dimension one, the branch link, its ideal-
psh candidate and envelope, its arbitrary ﬁnite-map pullback, its branch-surjective generic
trace and conductor descent, its ﬁnite conditional-expectation calculus, its ﬁnite-ﬂat canoni-
cal norm pushforward, and the principal-ideal range above, the independently geometric psh
and intersection-theoretic package is presently open.
    Two older local-volume questions should not be carried forward as open. For the
Boucksom–de Fernex–Favre local volume, Yuchen Zhang proves a positive dimension-
dependent lower bound for every nonzero volume of an isolated Gorenstein singularity and

constructs a non- Q-Gorenstein isolated singularity of volume zero that admits no boundary
making the pair log canonical [Zha14]. Thus the ﬁrst conjectural direction is conﬁrmed and
the second implication is disproved. These results delimit the singular theory above; they are
resolved history, not additional problems.
